title: Short-term happiness is improving across most countries while longer-run gains remain uneven, with relationships supporting happiness and finances driving unhappiness
geography: 29 countries; global, income and country comparisons

happy_global.unit: percent saying they are very or rather happy

unhappy_global.unit: percent saying they are not very or not at all happy

lower_income_happy.unit: percent of lower-income respondents saying they are happy

middle_income_happy.unit: percent of middle-income respondents saying they are happy

higher_income_happy.unit: percent of higher-income respondents saying they are happy

observations.method: Ipsos Global Advisor survey asking respondents whether they are very, rather, not very or not at all happy, with household-income comparisons.
observations.uncertainty: The global average is a simple country average and happiness is self-reported; income categories and cultural response styles are not directly comparable across all markets.
observations.subgroup: Adults under 75 in 29 countries, compared by household income.
observations.counterinterpretation: Income may proxy security, health, social position and local opportunity rather than independently causing happiness; country-level norms affect response intensity.

denominator.unit: countries in the 2026 Happiness Index; long-run comparison available for 20 countries

happier_than_last_year.unit: countries where people report higher happiness than 12 months earlier

less_happy_than_2011.unit: countries out of 20 comparable countries where reported happiness is lower than in 2011

turkiye_long_run_change.unit: percentage-point change in reported happiness since 2011

short_long_horizon_divergence.value: Short-term happiness improved in most surveyed countries while the longer-run series declined in most comparable countries

observations.method: Repeated Ipsos Happiness Index comparison across annual and long-run country series.
observations.uncertainty: The 12-month and 15-year comparisons involve changing country composition, survey context and macroeconomic conditions; they do not identify causes of trend movement.
observations.subgroup: Residents of 29 countries in 2026, with 20 countries in the long-run comparable series.
observations.counterinterpretation: Short-term rebounds may reflect temporary economic or political relief rather than reversal of deeper social, demographic or institutional pressures.

denominator.unit: adults under age 75 across 29 countries; analysis among respondents reporting happiness

feeling_appreciated_loved.unit: percent of happy respondents naming feeling appreciated or loved as contributing to happiness

family_relationships.unit: percent naming relationships with family and children as contributing to happiness

relationship_priority_pattern.value: Personal relationships are the strongest reported contributors to happiness

observations.method: Ipsos top-three selection of life areas contributing to reported happiness.
observations.uncertainty: The question identifies perceived contributors rather than causal effects; respondents may attribute happiness to salient relationships after the fact.
observations.subgroup: Respondents who reported being very or rather happy across 29 countries.
observations.counterinterpretation: Relationship answers may also capture material security, social support and cultural expectations rather than a separable interpersonal effect.

denominator.unit: adults under age 75 across 29 countries; analysis among respondents reporting unhappiness

financial_situation_unhappiness.unit: percent of unhappy respondents naming their financial situation as a source of unhappiness

financial_situation_top_in_28_countries.unit: countries out of 29 where financial situation is the leading reported source of unhappiness

mental_health_unhappiness.unit: percent naming mental health and wellbeing

housing_unhappiness.unit: percent naming housing situation or living conditions

external_cost_pattern.value: External financial and living-condition pressures drive unhappiness more consistently than social media or relationships

observations.method: Ipsos top-three selection of life areas contributing to reported unhappiness.
observations.uncertainty: The analysis is conditional on respondents who report unhappiness and does not measure clinical distress, debt, housing costs or causal pathways.
observations.subgroup: Respondents who reported being not very or not at all happy across 29 countries.
observations.counterinterpretation: Financial answers may be a broad frame for insecurity, health costs, housing, work and future uncertainty rather than a single spending problem.

related_sources.claim: Official Ipsos Happiness Index topic page describing the Global Advisor series.
Official Ipsos Happiness Index 2026 survey report PDF used for retrieval verification and hash.

boundary: This record adds a wellbeing-mechanism distinction: short-term happiness can improve while longer-run levels decline, relationships are perceived as the strongest happiness supports, and financial and housing pressures dominate unhappiness. It is a cross-national self-report survey, not a clinical mental-health measure, causal wellbeing model, longitudinal panel or population-weighted global happiness estimate.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Ipsos Happiness Index article, topic page and 2026 survey report PDF were retrieved and reviewed for sample, income gradient, country and time comparisons, happiness drivers and unhappiness sources; the PDF was hashed.
